newsitem.title: USA: Advocates seek to end annual U.S. debate on China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Advocates seek to end annual U.S. debate on China MFN.

text.p: Trade advocates hope to end what one White House official called a "corrosive" annual debate over U.S. trade relations with China as lawmakers look for other ways to address concerns about Beijing's policies.

The U.S. House of Representatives on Tuesday voted by a decisive 259-173 margin to renew China's Most Favoured Nation trade status. It was the second year in a row that the House backed MFN for China by a large majority and White House officials were quick to point to it as a sign of growing support for Clinton's policy of engagement.

"I think there is a growing consensus behind a policy of engagement," said White House national security adviser Sandy Berger. "We'll have to consult with leaders of Congress over the weeks and months ahead to see whether we can get out from under this annual debate, which tends to be rather corrosive of the relationship."

MFN trade status is given to almost every country in the world by the United States. Without it, tariffs on Chinese imports would soar to the high levels of the 1930's -- an average 44 percent from the current six percent.

Under U.S. law, the president each year must decide whether to grant China MFN and Congress has the right to disapprove his decision. Efforts to overturn the president's decision have failed every year since the 1989 crack-down on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.

Representative John Porter, an Illinois Republican who is co-chairman of the Congressional Human Rights Caucus and who in the past voted to revoke China's MFN status, said the annual debate has become a "pointless exercise" that cannot change Beijing's conduct.
This year he voted to back the president on MFN.

Instead of using the threat of ending MFN, which some trade advocates said would be the same as declaring economic war on China, Porter and Representative David Dreier, a California Republican, have developed a legislative package they said will more directly deal with U.S. concerns about human rights abuses, religious repression, missile and nuclear technology sales and the future of Hong Kong after July 1 when the British colony returns to Chinese rule.
The package includes money to beef up radio broadcasts to China and a measure that would deny visas to anyone implicated in human rights abuses or in proliferation of weapons.
One congressional aide said the package was designed to help pave the way for lawmakers to support permanent MFN status for China.
It is clear, though, that permanent MFN will be linked to to China's entry into the World Trade Organisation.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, plans to introduce legislation this week that calls for permanent MFN once Beijing makes a commercially acceptable offer to join the global trading system.

In the House, Nebraska Republican Doug Bereuter and Illinois Republican Thomas Ewing have sponsored legislation that would also give permanent MFN to China once it joined the WTO. But it also would set special interim duties on Chinese goods if U.S. exporters are denied adequate access to China's markets. The tariffs would not be anywhere near as high as the 1930's duties that would be imposed if China was denied MFN, but they would not be as beneficial as the MFN tariff rates.

The idea is to try to give Beijing an incentive to make the kinds of economic and legal reforms that would be necessary as a member of the global trading system. One-third of China's exports are earmarked for the United States.

But business leaders, who are anxious to end the annual ritual of reviewing China's MFN status, are worried that linking permanent MFN to China's WTO entry would take too long. U.S. officials have said that China still has a long way to go in making an acceptable offer to join the WTO.
